explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon brings his entire army and lays siege to Jerusalem (Jeremiah 39:1). A siege means he parks the army at the city and settles in. Nobody brings an entire army just to say hello.

I see why you'd think of a treaty, since that's how a lot of standoffs end. But verse 1 says Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem and laid siege to it. No treaty shows up in the verse. When the whole army marches in, the paperwork is not the first thing on the table.

Tribute is a payment to a stronger king, and it's a fair guess. But verse 1 doesn't mention any demand. It says Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched with his entire army and laid siege to the city. That's a lot more than an invoice.

Breached is right. On the ninth day of the fourth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year, the city was breached (Jeremiah 39:2). Zedekiah is the king of Judah, and the verse doesn't say how it happened. It just says the city was breached.
I get the hope in that one, but it's not what happened. Verse 2 says the city was breached. Jerusalem was not left alone. Babylon's army found a way in.

Surrender is what Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, had urged Zedekiah to do (Jeremiah 38:17). But verse 2 doesn't say the city surrendered. It says the city was breached, and Zedekiah's next move in verse 4 is to run.

The Middle Gate is right. The king of Babylon's officials came in and sat there (Jeremiah 39:3). Nergal-sharezer, Nebo-sarsekim and the rest of the officials took their seats in that gate. The verse names several of them.

Jerusalem does have a Fish Gate (Nehemiah 3:3), but that's not the gate this verse names. Verse 3 says the king of Babylon's officials sat in the Middle Gate. Easy to mix up when a city has this many gates. Stay with the Middle Gate and you're set.

The Sheep Gate is another gate in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:1), but this verse doesn't use it. The officials of the king of Babylon sat in the Middle Gate (Jeremiah 39:3). Gate names are a lot to keep straight, so no worries. Keep the Middle Gate in your pocket.

Not this time, friend. When Zedekiah king of Judah and his soldiers saw Babylon's officials, they fled (Jeremiah 39:4). Surrendering is what Jeremiah had urged (Jeremiah 38:17), but the verse says they ran instead. Seeing a guest list like that, I think running was the first idea that popped into their heads.

Right, it's false. The text says that when Zedekiah and all the soldiers saw the officials, they fled (Jeremiah 39:4). They didn't walk up and surrender. They left the city, and they didn't wait around to talk about it.

True. Verse 4 says they left the city at night. Zedekiah and his soldiers went out by way of the king's garden, through the gate between the two walls. They also took the route to the Arabah. You got it, baker.
It's actually true. Verse 4 says Zedekiah and the soldiers left the city at night, by way of the king's garden. Nothing in the verse says they left in daylight. They went out in the dark.

Jericho it is. The army of the Chaldeans, which is Babylon's army, caught up with Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho (Jeremiah 39:5). They overtook him and seized him. Running at night through the dark did not get him away.
Moab is a real place in the Bible (Ruth 1:1), but verse 5 doesn't name it here. The Chaldeans overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. He was heading toward the Arabah when they caught him.

Shinar is in the Bible (Genesis 11:2), so I get the guess. But the Chaldeans overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho (Jeremiah 39:5). He was headed toward the Arabah, and that army caught him on the way.

explanations.answer: To Riblah in the land of Hamath
explanations.explanation: Riblah is right. The Chaldeans seized Zedekiah and brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah in the land of Hamath (Jeremiah 39:5). That's where the king of Babylon was, and that's where he pronounced judgment. This is where the story gets heavy.

Carchemish is a real city on the Euphrates (Jeremiah 46:2), but it isn't what the verse says. Zedekiah was brought to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah in the land of Hamath (Jeremiah 39:5). Riblah is the name to remember.

explanations.answer: To Lachish in the land of Judah
explanations.explanation: Lachish was one of the cities of Judah (Jeremiah 34:7), which makes it a tempting answer. But verse 5 says they brought Zedekiah up to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah in the land of Hamath. That's far from home, in a different land altogether.
Babylon is right. Zedekiah was bound with bronze chains to be taken there (Jeremiah 39:7). It's the city of the king who defeated him. I think this is a hard place to stop and sit with for a second.
Egypt is a natural guess, friend. But verse 7 says the chains were to take Zedekiah to Babylon (Jeremiah 39:7). That's where Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom was centered.

Damascus is a fair guess, but this verse sends Zedekiah somewhere else. He was bound with bronze chains to be taken to Babylon (Jeremiah 39:7). Nice try, baker, but those chains had a Babylon address.

explanations.answer: The king's palace and the people's houses
explanations.explanation: That's right. The Chaldeans set fire to the palace of the king and to the houses of the people (Jeremiah 39:8). Two kinds of buildings are named there: the king's palace and the people's houses. Those are the ones the verse says burned.

explanations.answer: The king's garden and the city's gates
explanations.explanation: The garden does show up in this chapter, since Zedekiah slipped out by way of the king's garden (Jeremiah 39:4). But the fire in verse 8 is for the palace of the king and the houses of the people. The garden and gates aren't listed as burned.

explanations.answer: The Middle Gate and the guard's courtyard
explanations.explanation: Both of those places are named in this chapter, so it's easy to mix them up. The Middle Gate is where Babylon's officials sat (Jeremiah 39:3), and the courtyard of the guard is where Jeremiah was confined (Jeremiah 39:14). But verse 8 says the Chaldeans burned the palace of the king and the houses of the people.
Walls is right. The Chaldeans broke down the walls of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 39:8). The walls had kept Babylon outside for a long time, and now they were down. The siege had come to its end.
Markets sound like a reasonable thing for an army to go after, but verse 8 doesn't say that. It says the Chaldeans broke down the walls of Jerusalem. The walls were the city's protection.

The king's garden was how Zedekiah slipped out of the city (Jeremiah 39:4), so I see the connection. But verse 8 says the Chaldeans broke down the walls of Jerusalem. Walls are what you break down. Gardens are what you bring a rake to.

Poor is right. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left behind in the land of Judah some of the poor people who had no property (Jeremiah 39:10). Then he gave them vineyards and fields. People with no property were given land.

The nobles are the ones who were killed at Riblah (Jeremiah 39:6), so they weren't left in the land. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left some of the poor people who had no property (Jeremiah 39:10). Poor is the word in the verse.

I can see why a skilled worker might seem like a useful person to keep around. But verse 10 doesn't say skilled. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left some of the poor people who had no property.
True. At that time Nebuzaradan gave the poor people he left behind vineyards and fields (Jeremiah 39:10). People with no property were handed land to work. I bet that was quite a day for them.

It's true, so I understand the second thought. Verse 10 says that at that time Nebuzaradan gave the poor people he left behind vineyards and fields. They were left in the land of Judah with something to work.

explanations.answer: Look after him and let no harm come to him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Nebuchadnezzar's orders were, "Take him, look after him, and do not let any harm come to him…" (Jeremiah 39:12). Jeremiah is the LORD's prophet, and he had been confined in the courtyard of the guard. The king of Babylon gave an order to protect him.

explanations.answer: Take him to Babylon in bronze chains
explanations.explanation: The bronze chains were for Zedekiah (Jeremiah 39:7), so I see where that came from. Nebuchadnezzar's orders about Jeremiah were different: "Take him, look after him, and do not let any harm come to him…" (Jeremiah 39:12). The king of Babylon wanted him cared for, not chained.

explanations.answer: Keep him locked in the courtyard of the guard
explanations.explanation: Jeremiah had been confined in the courtyard of the guard (Jeremiah 39:15), so it's a fair guess. But the orders in verse 12 are "Take him, look after him, and do not let any harm come to him…" Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, was told to look after Jeremiah. Verse 14 says Jeremiah was brought from the courtyard of the guard and turned over to Gedaliah.
True. The orders end with, "do for him whatever he says." (Jeremiah 39:12). Nebuchadnezzar told Nebuzaradan to follow Jeremiah's lead. A king gave a prophet that kind of say.
It's true, friend. The orders from Nebuchadnezzar in verse 12 include, "do for him whatever he says." That means Nebuzaradan was told to do for Jeremiah whatever Jeremiah asked.

Take him home is right. The officials turned Jeremiah over to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, to take him home (Jeremiah 39:14). So Jeremiah remained among his own people. That's the simple, good ending to his time in the courtyard.
Carrying people to Babylon is what Nebuzaradan did with others (Jeremiah 39:9). But verse 14 says Gedaliah son of Ahikam was to take Jeremiah home. Jeremiah remained among his own people.

Jeremiah had been confined in the courtyard of the guard, so it's easy to think he'd stay under guard. But verse 14 says Gedaliah son of Ahikam was to take him home. That's a very different job from guarding.

explanations.answer: His words against the city will be fulfilled
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD said, "I am about to fulfill My words against this city for harm and not for good…" (Jeremiah 39:16). The message was for Ebed-melech the Cushite. The LORD said He would do what He had said.

explanations.answer: The city will be spared from all harm
explanations.explanation: I understand wanting a softer ending for the city. But the LORD said, "I am about to fulfill My words against this city for harm and not for good…" (Jeremiah 39:16). That's the message He gave Ebed-melech the Cushite.

explanations.answer: The city will be rebuilt right away
explanations.explanation: Rebuilding is a hopeful idea, but verse 16 doesn't say it. The LORD told Ebed-melech the Cushite, "I am about to fulfill My words against this city for harm and not for good…" The message is about fulfilling His words.

Not quite. The LORD said the opposite: "But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you will not be delivered into the hands of the men whom you fear." (Jeremiah 39:17). The message was for Ebed-melech the Cushite. The LORD promised to deliver him.

Right, it's false. The LORD told Ebed-melech the Cushite, "But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you will not be delivered into the hands of the men whom you fear." (Jeremiah 39:17). The men he feared would not get him. The LORD was the one doing the delivering.

explanations.answer: Because he trusted in the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD said, "Because you have trusted in Me, you will escape with your life like a spoil of war, declares the LORD." (Jeremiah 39:18). Ebed-melech the Cushite trusted Him, and the LORD gave him a promise. Trust is the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: Because he served the king well
explanations.explanation: I see why that sounds reasonable, friend. But the reason the LORD gave was different: "Because you have trusted in Me…" (Jeremiah 39:18). The text points to trust in the LORD.

explanations.answer: Because he left the city early
explanations.explanation: Verse 18 doesn't say anything about leaving early. The LORD told Ebed-melech, "Because you have trusted in Me, you will escape with your life like a spoil of war, declares the LORD." His reason was trust in the LORD.
